title: Lexicographically Smallest String After Applying Operations
statement:
You get a digit string `s` whose length is even, plus two integers `a` and `b`. Two moves are available, and you may use them as many times as you like (including zero) in any order:

- **Add**: every digit sitting at an odd index (0-based) grows by `a`, wrapping modulo 10, so `8 + 3` becomes `1`.
- **Rotate**: shift the whole string `b` places to the right, so its last `b` characters move to the front in the same order.

Return the lexicographically smallest string that can be produced. For two strings of equal length, the smaller one is the one holding the smaller digit at the first index where they disagree.
constraints: s contains only the digits 0 to 9
signature: String findLexSmallestString(String s, int a, int b)
notes:
## Intuition

Both moves are cycles: adding `a` ten times restores the odd digits, and rotating enough times restores the order. So only a limited set of strings can ever appear, at most 10 odd shifts × 10 even shifts × `n` rotations. Treat each string as a node of a graph whose two edges are the two moves, visit every reachable node once with BFS, and keep the smallest. (Enumerating rotation offsets and add counts directly also works and is the brute-force check.)

## Approach

1. Put `s` in `seen` and in `queue`; let `best` start as `s`.
2. Take strings from the front of the queue with the index `head`; if `current` beats `best`, replace it.
3. Build `added` by raising each odd-indexed digit by `a` modulo 10.
4. Build `rotated` by moving the last `b` characters to the front.
5. Enqueue each of the two neighbours that is not yet in `seen`, marking it as seen right away.
6. When the queue is exhausted, every reachable string was compared; return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "5525"`, `a = 9`, `b = 2`. Adding 9 is the same as subtracting 1 from the odd digits. From `"5525"` the BFS finds `"5424"` (add) and `"2555"` (rotate); `best` becomes `"2555"` once it is dequeued. Since `b` is even, rotations never move an even-index digit onto an odd index, so the reachable strings are the two rotations `"5525"` and `"2555"` with their odd digits shifted 0 to 9 times: 20 strings in all. Among them `"2555"` with its odd digits lowered five times, `"2050"`, is the smallest, and that is returned.

## Complexity

- Time: O(100 · n²): at most `100n` distinct strings, each built and hashed in O(n).
- Space: O(100 · n²) for `seen` and `queue`.

## Pitfalls

- Only odd indices change on an add; even digits change only after an odd rotation brings them to odd positions.
- Rotating right moves the tail to the front: `slice(-b) + slice(0, -b)`, not the other way round.
- Mark a string as seen when it is enqueued; both moves are cyclic, so without it the search never ends.
- Wrap with `% 10`; digits never carry into their neighbours.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `seen` | every string already discovered |
| `queue`, `head` | BFS queue and the index of the next string to process |
| `best` | smallest string dequeued so far |
| `current` | the string being expanded |
| `digits` | characters of `current`, edited for the add move |
| `added`, `rotated` | the two neighbours of `current` |
